item: Pulse is more important than note rate
content: 'The pulse is the key.' Many notes per second can feel sleepy when kick and snare are far apart; this took the energy out of live shows. The cure was the uneven grouping that listeners feel as a fast three.
parameters: Slow pulse 58 BPM = no dance feel. Felt three at 174 BPM = excited audience
where: Against the Fall of Night (title track)

item: Limits of rhythm perception that the band uses
content: Numbers that Neely gives for fast and slow limits.
parameters: Fastest spacing heard as rhythm: about 100 ms (grouping stops near 115 ms). Fastest practical dance tempo: about 240 BPM. Tempo that feels neither fast nor slow: about 100 BPM (600 ms). Walking: 60 BPM feels slow, 180 BPM feels fast
where: Neely videos 2021 to 2024

item: Small time shifts
content: Neely moved programmed drums about 20 ms off the grid and played the bass to fit. This felt more human than the quantised version. When both versions were made faster, the difference could not be heard.
parameters: Shift about 20 ms; the effect is lost at high speed
where: Demonstration in a 2023 video

item: 'Drunk' feel
content: The 'drunk' feel is a swing between straight and triplet swing, as in quintuplet swing and septuplet swing. Some drummers do not count it: they 'play drunk'. Dilla time mixes straight, swung and shifted parts, so that the layers of one groove have different feels.
parameters: Long note of the swing = 57 to 60 percent of the beat
where: Sequence Start; Dream of Mahjong; Drunk

item: Bass and drums
content: Neely's ideal for bass and drums: fluid and woven together, never rigid. His models: Paul Jackson and Mike Clark on Herbie Hancock's live album Flood; Gary Willis and Dennis Chambers.
parameters: 2 model rhythm sections
where: Interview 2025

item: Bright mood
content: A review: the complex writing keeps a bright, sunny, light mood, which is not usual in progressive music; a feel-good record with much groove. Neely calls the music 'silly jazz fusion'. The band wears coloured pyjamas or space costumes and tells jokes between pieces.
parameters: Database labels (algorithmic): high energy for 24 of 29 tracks; the top danceability label for 4 of 29; the lowest danceability label for 12 of 29
where: Perihelion (2021); concerts

item: Names for the style
content: Names in the sources: 'electro jazz duo' (Neely, 2019); 'electronic jazz fusion band' (Neely, 2023); 'electro-jazz/EDM group'; 'modern progressive jazz fusion'; a mix of 'jazz, progressive metal, and electronic music'; 'djazz' (for the 2017 cover). A blog gives the band's own line: 'too jazz for the rock guys, too rock for the jazz guys'. The name 'future jazz' was not found.
parameters: Bandcamp tags: edm, electronic, idm, livetronica, progressive, jazz fusion. Last.fm tags: jazz fusion, jazz, experimental, electronic, fusion, nu jazz
where: Descriptions 2017 to 2026
source: tvdb-electro; neely-grind; meinl-radio; discotech-radioeast; tvdb-wtwm; allthethings-atfon; bc-atfon; bc-atfon-single; lastfm-tags

item: Influences that the members name
content: Model for the duo: Evan Marien and Dana Hawkins (electronic music with jazz improvisation); Neely says that they inspired Sungazer to make music. Also named: Herbie Hancock (Flood), Tribal Tech, Allan Holdsworth, Rage Against the Machine, System of a Down, Victor Wooten, Knower, and Mike Mangini (Crowder's teacher). Neely's 2013 list: Meshuggah, Animals as Leaders, James Blake, Steve Reich, Ellington, Zappa, Mingus, Xenakis; bassist Tim Lefebvre.
parameters: Reviewers compare the band with Tigran Hamasyan, The Mars Volta, Mahavishnu Orchestra, Squarepusher and Aphex Twin (Neely: more the acts that those two influenced)
where: Interviews 2013 to 2025
source: ha-interview; notreble-2013; neely-cool7; tvdb-reharm; postmusic-live25; daddario-crowder

item: Why electronics
content: Neely in 2019: electronic music is 'the next wave for musical development'. The band still plays live and interacts with sampling and drum triggering; the electronic textures would be hard to get in other ways.
parameters: Live playing with sampling and drum triggering
where: Interview 2019

item: Groove first
content: The band calls its music "music for the brain and booty". League: the band "loves to groove" and is happy to groove with no melody and no solo. He connects the trance feel to West African music and to the large bands of Fela.
parameters: A groove with no melody and no solo is a permitted texture
where: Page of a film about the band; interview of 2023

item: Less bombast
content: League in 2019: the band writes for how the music feels to play, not for the excitement of virtuosity. The aim is "less bombast and more subtlety and depth". In 2025 he says that he does not want to write for the old, bombastic style.
parameters: Change of aim from about 2019
where: Immigrance; Somni

item: The Dallas change
content: When players from the Black gospel and R&B scene of Dallas joined, the music became funkier, tighter, simpler, and more emotional: "less cerebral" and more "visceral". The mentor of the band was the keyboard player Bernard Wright.
parameters: From about 2006-2007, when League met Bernard Wright in a Dallas church
where: Interviews of 2022 and 2023

item: A critical view
content: A critic: the virtuosity gives more excitement than depth. The music is a 'roller coaster' that leaves the listener at the start. The band improvises well but does not explore in its jams.
parameters: A warning for the new piece: speed must have a purpose
where: Column on the band

item: Risk in the live recording
content: A guitarist: "you have to make every take count". A mistake can stay on the record. One player plays safe to keep a good take; a different player wants to surprise the others in each solo. League: with the audience near, the band plays in a different way and is less afraid of mistakes.
parameters: No repair after the take on the live albums
where: Live albums with audience

item: Quantized but gritty
content: A "gritty, offbeat, but quantized kind of feel" from beat producers.
parameters: Models: Knxwledge, J Dilla, Madlib. He practised to quantized beats and to beats with no grid. DOMi: "don't take shit too seriously"

item: Full energy; dance music
content: The duo plays "full-blast" on all tracks. He calls the music dance music.
parameters: Loose technique for endurance. Influences named: James Brown, Skrillex (2009 to 2013), Boards of Canada, 16-bit game music

item: Human limit as value
content: Past a threshold, the human limit adds emotion and surprise to machine music.
parameters: Decisions in "fractions of seconds". "NERVE sounds like electronic music, but it's not."
where: TEDx talk; band text

item: Machine with soul
content: A drum machine "in the right hands can be as soulful as a saxophone".
parameters: Electronic music gives him "precision, discipline, timbral imagination"

item: Groove under the puzzle
content: The aim is groove, not counting. The listener should always find a quarter-note pulse. A short pattern repeated many times gives a trance effect.
parameters: Hagström: the rhythms are 'still an AC/DC song, just hidden'; he compares the music with funk. Abasi: imply an even metre and put the syncopation around it

item: Machine or human
content: The style sits between machine-like exactness and natural feel, and the players take sides.
parameters: Thall: copy a robot, no vibrato, takes edited from short pieces. Garstka: hard editing takes away the natural feel, so he posts unedited play-throughs. Meshuggah 2016: live takes with no edits

item: Where the heaviness comes from
content: Heaviness is not only distortion. It comes from syncopation, space, low register and small upward shifts.
parameters: With a dry thump tone: from syncopation. With very low tunings: from slow tempo and space. In Meshuggah: from a half-step shift of the riff and from fast kick under a slow snare. In Hamasyan: from the lowest octaves of the piano at a constant forte

item: Bright mood
content: The bright branch joins fast playing and djent riffs with a 'hip-shaking, jazzy' style. The mood is fun and uplifting.
parameters: Arch Echo name Rush, Allan Holdsworth, Weather Report, Animals as Leaders and video games as influences. Plini's Sunhead EP: the excitement of travel to new places. Plini names Snarky Puppy and Michael Jackson for one tune

item: Odd metres as a natural language
content: The time changes between machine-like runs of sixteenth notes and phrases that sit far behind the beat. Thought and emotion must be in balance.
parameters: 'You breathe odd meters.' Under a heavy riff he plays less, not more

item: Mystery and discipline
content: A mood of tension and expectation. The playing is not "free".
parameters: "consistently mysterious mood, an air of tense expectancy" (Coleman). Sun Ra: "My music is the music of precision"
where: Heliocentric Worlds Vol. 1; Other Planes of There

item: From heavy to light
content: The change from the space band to the funk band.
parameters: Sextant: "trance jazz". Head Hunters: he wanted "something lighter" and to feel "more tethered"
where: Sextant; Head Hunters

item: Groove, not time
content: The leader wants a groove with no backbeat on 2 and 4. He finds a sound first; the music follows from the sound.
parameters: Backbeat = "time", not rhythm. "rhythmic, bone-hard dance music". 13 volume pedals at his main keyboard station (1996)
where: Sweetnighter; later work

item: Words for the feel
content: Writers and players call the feel drunk, loose, limping and off-kilter. Dilla and T3 called it "simple-complex". Some drummers only think "play drunk".
parameters: Questlove when he first heard it: "The drums are messed up! The time is wrong!"
where: Reception

item: Planned imperfection
content: The grooves hang on the back of the beat. The band plays exactly and then adds a small error on purpose.
parameters: "deliberately insert the little glitch that makes it sound messed up"
where: Voodoo (2000)

item: Intense and dreamlike
content: One album aims at maximum speed and force. Another album aims at a dream state with tension and release.
parameters: "the fastest, hardest, most intense jazz record"
where: You're Dead!; Until the Quiet Comes

item: Liquid and digital
content: He wanted the music "totally liquid and psychedelic" and everything "brutal and digital".
parameters: Period of Go Plastic
where: Go Plastic (2001)

item: Dark, heavy, meditative
content: Dark tone, a large sub-bass that the body feels, sparse drums.
parameters: Motto of the DMZ label: "Come meditate on bassweight"
where: Deep dubstep

item: Aggressive and sudden
content: A calm start, then a drop that hits like metal music.
parameters: "lurching and aggressive"; the drop as "a load of bass bombs"
where: Skrillex; Excision

item: Drunk feel from odd subdivisions
content: The band makes the lopsided feel exact: the players count fives and sevens.
parameters: "Play lopsided tipsy grooves by subdividing in odd groupings"
where: Drunk (2018); video of 18 December 2018

item: Drummer swing ratio against tempo
content: The swing ratio of the ride cymbal changes gradually with tempo. It is as high as 3.5:1 at slow tempi. It reaches 1:1 at fast tempi. The 2:1 triplet feel occurs only at one tempo.
parameters: 3.5:1 (slow) to 1:1 (fast); 2:1 only at one tempo
where: Three well-known jazz recordings and a play-along record (abstract read)

item: The short eighth note has a floor of about 100 ms
content: The short note of the long-short pair stays at about 100 ms for medium to fast tempi. The authors see a practical limit on tone duration. A later corpus study found 110 to 80 ms and even 70 ms.
parameters: Short eighth: about 100 ms; range 70 to 110 ms; do not make it shorter
where: Ride cymbal patterns; tempi above about 150 BPM

item: Soloist: late downbeats, synchronised offbeats
content: At slow tempi the soloists play their downbeats after the cymbal. They are synchronised with the cymbal on the offbeats. Thus the swing ratio of the soloist is much smaller than that of the drummer.
parameters: Downbeat late; offbeat on time; soloist ratio < drummer ratio
where: Same recordings (abstract read; the paper gives the delays in graphs that were not seen)

item: Drummer swing ratio at 150, 250 and 300 BPM
content: Elvin Jones and Billy Higgins go from about 2.5 at about 150 BPM to about 1.5 at 250 BPM. Jones goes to about 1.0 at 300 BPM. Art Taylor and Carl Allen keep almost the same ratio at all tempi.
parameters: 150 BPM: about 2.5; 250 BPM: about 1.5; 300 BPM: about 1.0; some drummers: constant
where: 921 excerpts of the Weimar Jazz Database; 10 most frequent drummers

item: Drummer ratios in earlier studies
content: Rose found a mean rhythm-section ratio of 2.38 at about 130 BPM. Honing and de Haas found that drummers' ratios stabilise at around 2.2 below about 170 BPM. Ratios level off to 1.0 at about 300 BPM.
parameters: 130 BPM: 2.38; below 170 BPM: about 2.2; about 300 BPM: 1.0
where: Review of Rose (1989), Honing and de Haas (2008), Friberg and Sundström (2002)

item: Soloist swing ratios in earlier studies
content: All studies show soloist ratios well below 2.0. Rose: 1.05 to 1.89, mean about 1.43 at all tempi. Ellis: 1.474 to 1.871, grand mean 1.701. Busse: about 1.74. Armstrong: 1.61 and 1.58. A cluster near 1.0 above 260 BPM.
parameters: Soloist ratio 1.4 to 1.75 (mean values); near 1.0 above 260 BPM
where: Review of Rose (1985), Ellis (1991), Collier and Collier (2002), Busse (2002), Friberg and Sundström (2002)

item: Most soloist eighth-note pairs are nearly even
content: About 61% of 831 pairs have a ratio of 0.9 to 1.2. 79% are within 0.9 to 1.4. Only 19% are 1.5 or higher. The most frequent ratio is 1.2 for Adderley, Davis and Evans, and about 1.1 for Gordon and Coltrane.
where: Bill Evans, Cannonball Adderley, Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Dexter Gordon (shares calculated by Butterfield from Benadon's Figure 1)

item: The swing ratio goes up at the end of a phrase
content: Benadon sorts ratios into even (about 1.0), low (about 1.1 to 1.3) and high (1.4 and above). The ratio often increases at the end of a phrase. In one tune the ratios increase through the bar while the beat lengths decrease (r = -0.52).
parameters: Even 1.0; low 1.1 to 1.3; high 1.4+; raise the ratio on the last beats of a phrase
where: Coltrane, Konitz, Evans, Davis and others; 'Good Bait' (128 BPM)

item: Coltrane plays far behind the beat
content: Coltrane plays consistently behind the beat by roughly 50 to 80 ms. This is about a fifth of the beat.
parameters: +50 to +80 ms; about 20% of a beat at 200 BPM
where: 'I Hear a Rhapsody' (200 BPM), album Lush Life

item: Typical soloist swing ratio in 456 solos
content: Most soloists play only slightly uneven eighths: the ratio is 1.3:1. Ratios near 2:1 and higher are used only occasionally. High ratios are more likely at slow and moderate tempi and in postbop and hardbop.
parameters: Default soloist ratio 1.3:1; 2:1 or more only for effect
where: Weimar Jazz Database, 456 solos (abstract read)

item: Size of the soloist's downbeat delay
content: Many soloists delay their downbeats. The typical delay is about 30 ms, or 85 ticks of 960, at about 150 BPM. This is about 9% of a quarter note. The delay in ms becomes smaller at faster tempi. Most soloist swing ratios are below 1.5.
parameters: Downbeat delay 9% of a beat (30 ms at 150 BPM); soloist ratio < 1.5; ratio highest near 160 BPM
where: Weimar Jazz Database, 456 solos; drum downbeats as the reference

item: Late downbeats with on-time offbeats swing more
content: Jazz musicians rated three versions. Soloist downbeats delayed by 85 ticks with synchronised offbeats got the highest swing ratings: odds ratio 7.48 against the quantised version. A delay of all soloist notes gave no gain (p = 0.440).
parameters: Tempi 150, 168, 175 BPM; soloist ratio 1.65 to 1.7; rhythm section ratio 2.46 to 2.54
where: Piano recordings of 'Jordu', 'Texas Blues', 'The Smudge'

item: Timing spread and swing ratio of a pianist over a quantised rhythm section
content: The timing deviations are near normal with SD about 18.5 ms (plus or minus 2) at all tempi. The swing ratio falls with tempo. The mean note position is at most about 10 ms from the grid.
where: One professional pianist, 12 jazz standards, 130 to 190 BPM

item: Random deviations do not add swing
content: Quantised versions were rated slightly more swinging: odds ratio 1.65. Versions with doubled deviations were rated much lower: odds ratio 0.23. Inverted deviations were rated like the original.
parameters: Keep the unsystematic part small; never double it
where: Online survey, 160 listeners, 12 pieces

item: Swing ratio of piano soloists in trios
content: The mean log2 ratio is 0.34 (SD 0.59). This is about 1.27:1. 13.2% of the pairs are short-long. Oscar Peterson has the highest mean: log2 0.84, about 1.79:1. Faster performances swing less.
parameters: Mean ratio about 1.27:1; SD 0.59 in log2 units; 13% reversed pairs
where: JTD-300: 300 recordings by 10 pianists; 41,815 pairs

item: The piano soloist plays behind bass and drums
content: Pianists play 4.5% (SD 9.7) of a quarter note after the bassist and 6.0% (SD 9.3) after the drummer. Junior Mance: 2.0% after the drummer. Bud Powell: 10.4% after the drummer.
parameters: Lead after bass +4.5% of a beat; after drums +6.0%; SD about 9.5%. At 195 BPM: about +14 and +18 ms (conversion in this study)
where: JTD-300 piano trios; mean tempo 195 BPM

item: The soloist adapts to the rhythm section
content: The rhythm section is the anchor. Coupling coefficients: bass to piano 0.40; drums to piano 0.59; piano to bass 0.15; piano to drums 0.14. Self-coupling of the pianist: -0.52.
parameters: Lead corrects 40 to 60% of the last asynchrony; bass and drums correct about 15%
where: Linear phase correction models, 300 recordings

item: Ride cymbal and bass are almost together
content: The mean cymbal-bass asynchrony is +5.2 ms and -1.1 ms for the two bassists. By drummer it is +5.3, +1.4 and -0.1 ms. The authors found no systematic lead of bass or drums.
parameters: Mean ride-bass offset within about 5 ms
where: 3 drummers and 2 bassists; swing at 168 and 208 BPM

item: Pedal hi-hat early; ride and bass slightly late
content: The pedal hi-hat on beats 2 and 4 is 2 to 26 ms ahead of the pulse. The ride is after the hi-hat by 27.9, 13 and 8.6 ms for the three drummers. The bass is 7 to 26 ms after the hi-hat and 3 to 8 ms after the pulse.
parameters: Pedal hi-hat -2 to -26 ms; ride +8 to +28 ms after hi-hat; bass +3 to +8 ms after pulse
where: Jazz trio recordings with MIDI drums

item: Timing is tighter on the backbeats
content: All performers have a smaller timing spread on beats 2 and 4 than on beats 1 and 3.
parameters: Spread on 2 and 4 < spread on 1 and 3
where: Jazz trio recordings

item: Listeners prefer tightened jazz timing, not zero
content: Listeners (N = 26) preferred versions with the asynchronies reduced by 27.5% to 47.3%. In the preferred versions the bass and drum sounds are less than 19 ms apart. These beat the original and the fully quantised version.
parameters: Scale ensemble asynchrony to 50 to 70% of human size; keep bass-drum distance < 19 ms
where: 12 excerpts; original, reduced and increased asynchrony

item: Funk duo against a click: offsets and spread by instrument
content: Medians: hi-hat -3 ms, snare -4 ms, bass -3 ms, bass drum -12.5 ms (early). SD: hi-hat 10.3 ms, bass drum 10.5 ms, snare 15.9 ms, electric bass 18.8 ms. All events: -46 to +58 ms, SD 15.3 ms.
parameters: Kick 12.5 ms early; SD 10 ms (hi-hat, kick), 16 ms (snare), 19 ms (bass)
where: Professional drums and bass, 100 BPM, 214 events in 20 s (one text passage gives SD 5.3 ms; 15.3 ms agrees with the other values)

item: Swing duo against a click: offsets and spread by instrument
content: Swing ratio 2.66:1. Medians: bass -17.5 ms, ride -14 ms, pedal hi-hat -33 ms, snare 0 ms. All events: -67 to +85 ms, SD 22.8 ms. Over both clips: bassist SD 23.4 ms, drummer SD 17.7 ms; the bassist is 2 ms ahead of the drummer (not significant).
parameters: Ride -14 ms; bass -17.5 ms; pedal hi-hat -33 ms; snare 0 ms; SD 22.8 ms
where: Professional drums and bass, 150 BPM, 157 events in 20 s

item: Experts move most at 40% of the played deviations
content: Expert listeners moved their heads more to clips with the deviations reduced by 60% than to quantised clips. At this level the SD is 9.1 ms in swing and 6.1 ms in funk.
parameters: Target SD: 6 ms (funk, 100 BPM); 9 ms (swing, 150 BPM)
where: 160 listeners (79 experts); motion capture

item: Best groove at about 40% of performed microtiming; never exaggerate
content: Quantised and original timing were rated equally high. Ratings fell for exaggerated timing. Quadratic models put the best groove at about -60%, halfway between quantised and original. Experts were irritated from +40%; non-experts from +80%.
parameters: Scale 0.4 (best); 0 to 1.0 safe; 1.4 irritates experts; 1.8 irritates all
where: Funk at 100 BPM and swing at 150 BPM; 79 experts and 81 non-experts

item: Performed microtiming is about 10% of the mean inter-onset interval
content: RMS deviation from the grid: 27.2 ms in the swing clip and 15.7 ms in the funk clip. As a share of the mean inter-onset interval: 10.64% and 9.11%. As a share of the beat: 0.068 and 0.026.
parameters: RMS deviation = 0.10 x mean inter-onset interval (as performed); x 0.4 for best groove = 0.04
where: Same swing and funk duo recordings

item: Irregular drums hurt; a bass-drums offset does not
content: Listeners (n = 160) reacted negatively to fixed displacements inside the drum track. A fixed displacement of the whole bass track against the drums had no effect. Fixed snare shifts irritated experts more than played deviations.
parameters: Snare shifts of 8, 16, 24 ms: negative; bass-drums shift up to 62.5 ms: no effect
where: Swing and funk duo recordings

item: A shifted snare or bass drum lowers the groove
content: Shifts of -25, -15, +15 and +25 ms were tested. The quantised version rated highest. Larger shifts rated lower. Early shifts rated worse than late shifts. Snare shifts rated worse than bass drum shifts.
parameters: If one drum is shifted: late is better than early; kick tolerates more than snare; 15 ms is already audible
where: Simple rock drum pattern; 93 music students (abstract read)

item: Systematic microtiming lowers groove ratings
content: Idiomatic microtiming from nil to about double the natural level lowered groove, liking and naturalness. The exception was the simple short-long shuffle jazz pattern. The effect was stronger for expert listeners.
parameters: Only the long-short swing pattern itself helps
where: Synthesised jazz, funk and samba patterns (abstract read)

item: Bass after drums is preferred over bass before drums
content: Bass-drums asynchronies from -80 to +80 ms increased mental effort and lowered tapping stability. Listeners preferred on-the-grid grooves, except in the condition nearest to real music. Bass after drums was preferred over the reverse.
parameters: If the bass is offset, put it late; a steady 8th-note hi-hat makes the groove easier
where: Jazz musicians and non-musicians; pupil size and tapping (abstract read)

item: Bass-drums discrepancies of 30 ms or less are hard to hear
content: Two experiments gave little support for the idea that bass-drums asynchrony drives swing. Most listeners could not consistently identify discrepancies of 30 ms or less.
parameters: Detection limit about 30 ms for bass-drums lead or lag
where: Synthetic swing groove and recordings of professionals (abstract read; the 30 ms value is read in Kilchenmann and Senn)

item: The ride tap falls ahead of the bass
content: At about 180 BPM one drummer's ride pick-up note was about 33% of the beat and another's about 25%. The ride tap was ahead of the bass on most beats. Two players moved in and out of phase with the bass in cycles.
parameters: Pick-up at 33% (ratio 2:1) or 25% (ratio 3:1); ride ahead of bass
where: Play-along recording and experiments with a recorded bass line (text excerpt read)

item: 16th-note swing in classic drum breaks is small
content: Sixteenth-note swing was common in 30 classic drum breaks but often subtle: median ratio 1.2:1. The size of the swing was not correlated with tempo. A backbeat delay was frequent at beat 2 but not at beat 4.
parameters: 16th swing 1.2:1 = 54.5% (conversion in this study); delay the snare on beat 2 only
where: 30 drum breaks of the breakbeat canon (abstract read)

item: A laid-back snare is about 17 ms late and louder
content: Ten expert drummers played laid-back, on-the-beat and pushed. A majority played the laid-back strokes louder than the on-the-beat strokes. Higher tempo gave a higher sound level. At 96 BPM the laid-back snare was 17.4 ms late on average.
parameters: Laid-back snare: +17 ms and louder; pushed: earlier
where: Rock pattern at three tempi (abstract read; the 17.4 ms value is read in Carter and von Appen)

item: Drummers: timing styles against a click and against a track
content: 22 drummers played laid-back, pushed and on-beat. Onsets followed the instruction on hi-hat, snare and kick. An instrumental backing track gave larger shifts than a metronome. The metronome gave earlier mean onsets. Snare length and snare and hi-hat loudness changed with the style.
parameters: Mean laid-back snare delay about 17 ms; SD of strokes 11 to 19 ms, smaller at faster tempi
where: Back-beat pattern and a complex variation (abstract read; the ms values are read in Carter and von Appen)

item: Guitar and bass: the timing style changes the sound
content: 21 guitarists and 21 bassists played laid-back, on-the-beat and pushed. Laid-back guitar strokes were longer and darker (lower spectral centroid). Pushed bass strokes were louder than on-the-beat and laid-back strokes.
parameters: Laid-back: longer, darker; pushed: louder, shorter
where: Simple pattern with a metronome (abstract read)

item: Two beat positions 50 to 80 ms apart in one groove
content: In part 2 of the groove the layers give two alternative beat positions about 50 to 80 ms apart. The perceived beat moves toward the added onsets. The half note becomes an added level of entrainment.
parameters: Wide beat: two onsets 50 to 80 ms apart on one beat
where: D'Angelo, 'Left & Right' (abstract read)

item: Size of a delayed backbeat on record
content: In 'Monkey Man' beat 2 is always late, by 10 to 80 ms, mean 28 ms. Beat 4 is late by 9 ms on average. The SD of the beat 2 placement is 10 to 20 ms. In 1967 to 1973 the mean delay was 2.4% of the beat on beat 2 and 1.7% on beat 4.
parameters: Beat 2: +28 ms (10 to 80); beat 4: +9 ms; SD 10 to 20 ms; 2.4% and 1.7% of a beat
where: Charlie Watts; 81 Rolling Stones recordings

item: Tempo drift and stability of jazz trios
content: Mean tempo slope: +0.02 BPM per second (SD 0.04). Tempo stability: 26.2 ms (SD 10.4), about 9% of a quarter note at the mean tempo of 195 BPM. Faster performances are more stable.
parameters: Drift +0.02 BPM/s (SD 0.04): about +6 BPM in 5 minutes (conversion in this study); local beat SD about 9% of a beat
where: 300 piano trio recordings

item: Tempo variability of a band without a click
content: Tempo CV is the SD of the local tempo divided by the mean, in percent. With a drum machine: 0.29. Median by period: 1.23, 1.94 and 0.96. Values of 2.0 or more show a freer approach. On one live album all 23 tracks speed up; the largest increase is 48%.
parameters: CV 0.3 (machine); 1.0 to 1.3 (steady band); 2.0+ (free); live drift up to +48%, most tracks +5 to +15%
where: 133 studio and 28 live Rolling Stones recordings; 304 recordings by other artists

item: Where a band speeds up and slows down
content: The band speeds up at the end of a verse into the chorus and comes back down for the next verse. Bridges and breakdowns are slower. Fuller texture goes with faster tempo. The drummer speeds up slightly in fills. Bands speed up much more often than they slow down.
parameters: Push into the chorus; relax in the breakdown; rush fills slightly; net drift is upward
where: Rolling Stones studio recordings; one tune goes from 78 to 107 BPM (+37%)

item: Timing error against a metronome is long-range correlated
content: The deviations from the click are Gaussian. A professional drummer at 180 BPM: mean -16.4 ms, SD 15.6 ms. Lowest SD about 12 ms; average about 21 ms. The power spectrum follows 1/f^beta with beta from 0.2 to 1.3. Complex drum patterns: beta 0.8 to 1.1.
parameters: SD 12 to 21 ms; beta 0.8 to 1.1 for drum patterns (0.2 to 0.5 for voice); deviations > 100 ms in < 0.5%
where: Drummers, singers and tappers with a click at 124 to 190 BPM

item: Listeners prefer 1/f humanising to white-noise humanising
content: Both versions had deviations with SD 15 ms. Listeners chose the 1/f version in 64.1% of the pairs (p < 0.002). 79.1% judged the 1/f version to be more precise.
parameters: Use 1/f noise (beta = 1), SD 15 ms or less; not white noise
where: Pop song, 39 listeners

item: Hi-hat 16ths of a studio drummer without a click
content: Mean 16th-note interval 156.6 ms at 96 BPM; SD 8.7 ms, Gaussian. Lag-1 correlation of the intervals: -0.48. The DFA exponent is 0.31 below about 5 to 8 s and 0.72 above. For the amplitudes it is 0.63. The pulse drifts on a 300 ms scale; the tempo changes at section borders.
parameters: Interval SD 8.7 ms = 5.6% (conversion in this study); neighbours anticorrelated (-0.48); slow drift correlated (0.72); amplitude 0.63
where: Jeff Porcaro, 'I Keep Forgettin'' (1982), one-handed hi-hat

item: Beat-interval spread in 100 jazz and rock recordings
content: SD of the beat intervals: 13.1 ms without a click and 11.5 ms with a click. Jazz 14.3 ms and rock/pop 11.9 ms without a click. The slow tempo process has exponent 0.54 (SD 0.38). The note-level process dominates below about 8 beats.
parameters: Beat SD 11 to 15 ms; note-level noise < 8 beats; slow drift beyond; jazz looser than rock
where: 47 jazz and 53 rock/pop recordings; cymbal beats

item: Two players' deviations follow each other for minutes
content: The beat intervals of two people who play together have scale-free cross-correlations. The next beat of one player depends on the history of the other player's intervals for up to several minutes.
parameters: Couple the slow drift of the parts; do not use independent noise for each part
where: Pairs of musicians and laypeople (abstract read)

item: The limbs differ against a click
content: At 60 and 120 BPM the hi-hat hand is within about 2 ms of the click. The snare hand and the kick foot are about 10 ms early. At 200 BPM the hi-hat hand is about 10 ms late and snare and kick are within about 1 ms. The errors of the limbs are correlated.
parameters: Kick and snare 10 ms before the hi-hat at 60 to 120 BPM; hi-hat 10 ms late at 200 BPM
where: 15 professional drummers; basic pattern (abstract read)

item: A large part of drum microtiming is a repeating pattern
content: Up to 65 percent of the total microtiming variability is explained by recurring and consistent patterns. The remainder is residual variability.
parameters: Systematic pattern up to 0.65 of the variance; random part 0.35 or more
where: MIDI drum kit performances and professional recordings (abstract read)

item: An accent lengthens the interval that follows it
content: Players raise the stick higher before an accented stroke. The interval that starts with the accented stroke is lengthened. The timing shows a slow drift and a short-term flutter between adjacent intervals.
parameters: After an accent: longer interval; drift + flutter
where: Three professional percussionists and one amateur (abstract read)

item: On the piano the louder voice sounds about 30 ms early
content: The emphasised voice is about 30 ms ahead of the other voices at the hammer. At the key the lead is almost zero. The lead is an effect of the higher key velocity.
parameters: Louder chord note: up to 30 ms earlier (acoustic piano)
where: 22 pianists, computer-monitored grand piano (abstract read)

item: Mean distance of drum hits from the 16th-note grid
content: A quantised score has a mean absolute timing error of 22.6 ms against the human performance. Notes on the eighth-note positions are more often late. Notes off the eighth-note positions are more often early.
parameters: Mean absolute offset 22.6 ms (all notes, all styles)
where: Groove MIDI Dataset, test set

item: Spread and offset of backbeat, kick and hi-hat against the click
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Backbeat snare: robust SD 15.1 ms, mean -9.8 ms. Kick on beats 1 and 3: 16.5 ms and -13.7 ms. Closed hi-hat 8ths: 15.6 ms and -9.2 ms. Medians over files.
parameters: SD 15 to 17 ms; drummers 9 to 14 ms ahead of the click; kick earliest
where: 4/4 beats in groove styles by the four drummers with 83% of the data; 178 to 206 files

item: Snare and kick are slightly ahead of the hi-hat
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). In the same 16th slot the backbeat snare is 5.2 ms before the hi-hat and the kick 6.8 ms before it (medians over files). Pooled SD of kick minus hi-hat: 15.2 ms; snare minus hi-hat: 19.5 ms.
parameters: Kick -7 ms, snare -5 ms against the hi-hat; SD between limbs 15 to 20 ms
where: 4/4 beats in groove styles

item: Timing offsets drift; they are not white noise
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Lag-1 autocorrelation of the hi-hat offsets against the click: +0.57 (quartiles 0.42 to 0.67). For the backbeat snare: +0.21. For the hi-hat velocities: -0.20.
parameters: Offset noise: positive correlation from note to note; velocity alternates
where: 4/4 beats in groove styles; 178 files

item: Ghost notes are at about 0.28 of the backbeat velocity
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Ghost notes: mean velocity 32 (quartiles 27 to 37), SD 11.5. Accented backbeats: mean 122, SD 7.7. Ratio 0.28 (quartiles 0.22 to 0.33). There are 1.8 ghost notes for each backbeat (quartiles 0.75 to 3.3).
parameters: Ghost velocity = 0.28 x backbeat (0.22 to 0.33); backbeat SD 6% of full scale
where: 133 files with ghost notes; MIDI velocity 1 to 127 of an electronic kit, not dB

item: Snare velocities have two peaks
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Snare hits off the backbeat: median velocity 46 (quartiles 29 to 103); 41% are below 40 and 30% are 90 or more. In funk 51% are below 40. Backbeat hits: median 127.
parameters: Two classes: ghost (20 to 45) and accent (100 to 127); few hits between
where: 372 beat files in groove styles; 53 funk files

item: Hi-hat accents by 16th-note position
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Mean closed hi-hat velocity on the beat, on the 'and', and on 'e' or 'a'. Groove styles: 87, 69, 54. Funk: 84, 63, 38. Hip-hop: 98, 65, 48. SD of the on-beat strokes inside a file: 21.
where: 4/4 beats; closed hi-hat

item: Fills get louder and rush a little
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). A fill has a median of 17 notes in 3.4 beats: 8.8 notes per second (quartiles 7.4 to 10.4). The velocity rises in 79% of the fills: from 70 in the first third to 88 in the last third. The timing moves early by 2.7 ms per beat; 66% of the fills rush.
parameters: Fill: 7 to 10 notes/s; crescendo +27%; rush 2.7 ms per beat
where: 533 fills by the four main drummers, played to a click

item: Flams and drags: 30 to 50 ms between the strokes
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Jazz: snare pairs are 29 ms apart (quartiles 21 to 37); the first stroke is softer in 68% (velocity 40, then 73). Funk: 17.6% of the snare hits are in soft pairs 39 ms apart (quartiles 31 to 48; velocity 34 and 28): drags or double ghost strokes.
parameters: Flam gap 20 to 40 ms, grace at 0.55 of the main stroke; drag gap 30 to 50 ms, both soft
where: 48 jazz and 53 funk beat files

item: Loudness and timing are not linked in the hi-hat
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). The slope of timing offset against velocity for hi-hat 8ths is -0.01 ms per velocity unit (quartiles -0.08 to +0.06). Loud strokes are not systematically early or late.
parameters: No loud-late rule for the hi-hat; use the rules for accents and laid-back strokes instead
where: 178 beat files in groove styles

item: Most played 16ths are straight; a minority are swung
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Swing ratio of the closed hi-hat 16ths per file: median 1.01; upper quartile 1.11; 90th percentile 1.42.
parameters: Straight 16ths in about 75% of the grooves; 1.1 to 1.4 in the rest
where: 124 beat files in groove styles with 16th hi-hats

item: Medium syncopation gives the most groove
content: The relation between syncopation and the wish to move is an inverted U. Medium syncopation gives the most desire to move and the most pleasure. A second study with piano melodies found the same.
parameters: Medium syncopation; not none, not maximum
where: 50 funk drum breaks at 120 BPM, 66 listeners; synthesised melodies

item: What predicts groove in 248 drum patterns
content: Syncopation (R2 = 0.010) and event density (R2 = 0.011) raise the ratings a little. Residual microtiming, beat salience and rhythmic variability have no effect. The listener's style bias (R2 = 0.123) and familiarity are much stronger.
parameters: Density and syncopation help; residual microtiming does not
where: 248 drum patterns from pop, rock, funk, metal, hip hop, soul, R&B; 665 listeners

item: Event density and beat salience, not microtiming
content: Event density between the beats and the salience of the beat correlate strongly with groove. Microtiming plays no significant role. Musicians who want more groove add notes on faster metrical levels and syncopation.
parameters: More notes between beats; clear beat; syncopation
where: 100 music examples from five genres; a performance study with four musicians (abstracts read)

item: Best tempo for groove
content: Drum breaks were tested at six tempi from 60 to 200 BPM. The optimal tempo for groove was about 100 to 120 BPM.
parameters: 100 to 120 BPM
where: Drum breaks (abstract read)

item: Uneven subdivisions can be as tight as even ones
content: In Malian jembe music the beat is divided short-long-long. The timing precision and coordination are the same as in a piece with even subdivisions.
parameters: A stable non-isochronous subdivision is a valid grid
where: 15 performances; about 43,000 onsets (abstract read)

item: Smallest timing change that listeners hear
content: For intervals below about 240 ms the threshold is about 10 ms; another source gives 6 ms. For 240 to 720 ms it is about 4.5% of the interval. Another study gives 2.5% of the beat for 60 to 200 BPM, and 4.4% for untrained listeners.
parameters: 6 to 10 ms (fast notes); 2.5 to 4.5% of the interval (slower notes)
where: Reviews of ten Hoopen et al., Friberg and Sundberg, Madison and Merker
